title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] Ok -- as promised, more about uncertainty quantification. Suppose we are sequentially making predictions in a k-class setting: We see images that could be hot dogs, stop signs, rabbits, etc. If we are unsure of a label, we should produce a set of labels --- a "prediction set".
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F-MUmY-WgAARtpD.jpg
────────
[2/7] We want prediction sets to be small, but also to cover the true label 90% of the time. If our predictor's "class scores" were true probabilities, this would be easy: Sort the class probabilities from highest to lowest, and include labels until their scores sum to at least 90.
────────
[3/7] The problem: Class scores aren't probabilities, so this doesn't work. And with k labels, there are 2^k possible prediction sets... It would be enough that the class scores were calibrated --- but k-dimensional calibration has exponential computational and statistical complexity.
────────
[4/7] This can be done with running time and statistical complexity only linear in k, and the result is that the scores can be used as if they were probabilities for the downstream prediction set task. What's more, we can calibrate to multiple downstream tasks at the same time.
────────
[5/7] We give a different approach: Given a method for converting probabilities to prediction sets (like sorting and taking the top 90% of the mass), we produce class scores that are unbiased conditional on the decision of the prediction set algorithm to include each label.
────────
[6/7] Ok -- we get strong coverage guarantees. But are the predictions any good? Well if you have some way (e.g. a pretrained NN) for obtaining "good" predictions, we can layer on all of our guarantees onto your method while only improving the cross entropy (or any other proper loss).
────────
[7/7] The paper is here: the prediction set guarantees are the last application.

summary:
[1/6] We'd like LLM outputs to be accompanied by confidence scores, indicating the confidence we should have in them. But what semantics should a confidence score have? A minimal condition is calibration: e.g. when we express 70% confidence, we should be correct 70% of the time. But...
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GKuW2xiWoAAvklK.jpg
────────
[2/6] LLM prompts can be very different. A model might be much more likely to hallucinate when asked for citations to the functional analysis literature vs. when asked for state capitals. Calibrated models can be systematically over-confident for one and under-confident for the other.

[1/8] Something that puzzles me about the conformal prediction literature: It is very focused on getting O(1/n) coverage bounds -in expectation- over the calibration set, rather than O(1/sqrt{n}) coverage bounds -conditional on- it. But in what applications is this the right guarantee?

[2/8] These cancellations make the bounds prettier. But to take advantage of them in applications where you want coverage, you'd need a new calibration set for every prediction that you made. Whenever you repeatedly re-use a fixed calibration set, you don't enjoy these cancellations.

[5/8] In that case, you observe the conditional coverage bounds, conditional on your (fixed) calibration set. So here the correct bounds are on the order of 1/sqrt{n}. This strikes me as the primary use case, at least in ML applications. But there is little focus on this kind of bound.
────────
[6/8] (My curmudgeonly gripes are best focused on split conformal methods where there is a calibration set --- I have thought less hard about what the right high probability coverage bounds are for full conformal --- but maybe someone else has. Not at all clear it should be 1/n)

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] The Sherman Act (1890) was written to prevent old fashioned price fixing: picture two men meeting in a smoky bar. It requires overt communication of intent to coordinate on prices. But pricing algorithms can automatically coordinate on high prices. What is algorithmic collusion?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GXCMUTmbEAAB_O0.jpg
────────
[2/8] So what kind of algorithms come up with reasonable prices but don't encode threats? "No regret learning algorithms" seem pretty innocuous --- they straightforwardly play a smooth best respond to the empirical pricing history. Its hard to imagine a less threatening algorithm.
────────
[3/8] It is hard to define. Simply arriving at high prices is not enough: An economic rule of thumb has been that "algorithmic collusion" requires threats: think folk-theorem strategies that will sustain high prices so long as your competitor does, but punishes them when they defect.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GXCMhhvbAAA7whU.png
────────
[4/8] A sub-class of these algorithms, called "no swap-regret" algorithms have even stronger guarantees, and are guaranteed to converge to competitive prices if both parties use them. Swap regret has been previously proposed as a proxy to detect anti-competitive behavior.
────────
[5/8] In fact, since random prices already lead to near monopoly profits for them, this will happen even if they take care to optimize only over non-responsive strategies, which are independent of the other seller's actions. Such strategies definitionally cannot encode threats.
────────
[6/8] Suppose the second entrant goofs up and forgets to run their RL algorithm, and just uses a uniformly random pricing strategy. This will lead to near monopoly profit. Of course if they don't forget to run their algorithm and optimize better than this, prices will only be higher.
────────
[7/8] In other words, neither player is employing threats, both players are best responding to the other in the space of all algorithms they could play, and yet prices are sustained near the monopoly level. We think this complicates how to think about algorithmic collusion.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GXCQDaLbAAAj6Ie.png
────────
[8/8] This is joint work with @EshwarERA, @natalie_collina, Sampath Kannan, and @JubaZiani. The paper is here:

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Is the distinction between "aleatoric" and "epistemic" uncertainty practically meaningful (or even well defined) in any real sense? Aleotoric uncertainty refers to irreducible unpredictability (e.g. unrealized randomness in nature) whereas epistemic refers to model uncertainty.
────────
[2/8] But note that there is no way to distinguish the two empirically: Suppose the world is such that the probability of rain every day is 1/2. Alternately, suppose the probability of rain is 1 or 0 every day, but selected at random. And suppose I predict p = 1/2 every day.
────────
[3/8] It is hard for me as a computer scientist to put lots of importance on a distinction that has no observational consequences. At a more fundamental level, whether uncertainty is epistemic or aleotoric seems to have everything to do with our model and nothing to do with the world.
────────
[4/8] In the first case my model is correct and the uncertainty is all aleatoric. In the second case there is in fact no aleatoric uncertainty and my uncertainty is epistemic. But of course the two scenarios are observationally equivalent --- there is no way to distinguish the two.
────────
[5/8] Anyhow lots of people seem to think it is important so I'm willing to believe my thinking is naive. What is the case for this distinction being of first order importance?
────────
[6/8] We think of coin flips as being random (pure aleotoric uncertainty) but that is only because we don't measure the initial conditions accurately enough and perform the necessary computations. If we did the aleotoric uncertainty vanishes. So maybe the uncertainty is epistemic.
────────
[7/8] Deciding when to devote resources to reduce uncertainty is important but this is true even if all uncertainty is epistemic --- the marginal cost of reducing uncertainty can vary widely (e.g. the coinflip example) and it might not always be your best return on invesment.
────────
[8/8] @KordingLab Generally it will not be possible to determine from data if the world is inherently random or if you have not uncovered the correct patterns in the data to explain the outcomes.

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] Suppose you and I both have different features about the same instance. Maybe I have CT scans and you have physician notes. We'd like to collaborate to make predictions that are more accurate than possible from either feature set alone, while only having to train on our own data.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoF3PaBWoAAZS15.png
────────
[2/9] Why? Maybe our features are mutually illegible: e.g. maybe I'm a person and you are a neural network. Or maybe I'm geared up to learn on visual data and you are geared up to learn on text data --- neither of us can easily learn on both. Or maybe regulation prevents data sharing.
────────
[3/9] We showed in our STOC 2025 paper ( that if both parties engage in such conversations and are calibrated conditional on what their counter-party said at the previous round that they quickly converge to agreement, generalizing Aumann's agreement theorem.
Quoting @Aaroth
I'm excited about a new paper that gives tractable generalizations of Aumann's Agreement Theorem, with an eye towards human/model collaboration in machine learning. We can implement algorithms that can "converse" with people and quickly come to agreement on downstream actions. 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GdzrX2daAAAvul6.png
────────
[4/9] Can we have conversations in which we exchange predictions, and quickly converge to predictions that not just agree, but are as accurate as the best predictor in a class that has access to our joint feature space, even though neither of us has access to the other's features? Yes.
────────
[5/9] In our new paper, what we show is that if both parties further have no swap regret (are "multicalibrated") with respect to function classes H(A), H(B) defined on their own features, then we can give accuracy guarantees with respect to a joint function class H(J).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoF6SYZW4AAOwtQ.jpg
────────
[6/9] For any function classes H(A), H(B), H(J) satisfying this weak learning condition, we show how two parties can collaborate to be as accurate at H(J), by only needing to solve a small number of squared error regression problems on their own data over H(A) and H(B) respectively.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoF5j9OXEAA62sv.jpg
────────
[7/9] H(A) and H(B) are weak learners wrt H(J) if, whenever learning over H(J) can improve on constant prediction, learning over H(A) or H(B) can as well. It turns out linear functions over XA and linear functions over XB are weak learners wrt linear functions over the joint features.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoF5OscW8AAXXtD.jpg
────────
[8/9] Just as our last paper generalized Aumann's agreement theorem, this paper tractably generalizes "information aggregation" theorems for Bayesian reasoners. Our results lift back to the classic Bayesian setting and give the first distribution free information aggregation theorems.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoF5y_hWUAAo1bi.jpg
────────
[9/9] The paper is here: and is joint work with the excellent Natalie Collina, Ira Globus Harris, @SurbhiGoel_ Varun Gupta, and Mirah Shi!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GoF4xiPWgAAjvc6.jpg

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] To contribute to common knowledge :-) I too have been integrating AI tools closely into my research. This paper with @mkearnsupenn and Emily was my first experiment with this, and it was just accepted to SODA. I'll describe the process in thread.
Quoting @minilek
I’ve also been integrating LLMs into my research workflow. I spent most of Tuesday working on a problem I’ve been thinking about for a while with some collaborators. I had a conjecture on a possible way forward, and with some hours of thinking, mixing in conversations with Gemini to guide certain non-trivial calculations, Gemini ultimately spit out a proof that no approach in this family can possibly work (which I found surprising, since similar approaches worked in related settings).
Maybe will say more about what the problem is after it’s fully resolved, lest I lead to us getting scooped. :) tl;dr LLMs haven’t replaced me (yet?), but certainly are making me a more efficient researcher.
*work still ongoing*
────────
[2/13] It would then expand these informal arguments into formal lemma and theorem statements, directly in the tex documents we were working in. It would provide proofs. It had access to all of the tex docs for the paper which was useful for keeping it notationally consistent, etc.
────────
[3/13] The first draft of all of the math (prelims, lemmas, theorems) was all done in the Windsurf environment, using Gemini 2.5 Pro. We would describe mathematical arguments to it as we would to a colleague without a whiteboard: intuitions and high level arguments, but no calculations.
────────
[4/13] Mostly we had the theorems in our head already, but sometimes Gemini would prove a lemma in a surprising way, simplify an argument, or improve some bounds. When we tried to get it to prove stuff that we didn't know how to prove it would often take us down rabbit holes.
────────
[5/13] We would verify correctness of each intermediate step before moving on. Generally if we gave it the kind of high level argument a colleague would understand, it would provide a formal proof without error. When it did make errors they were human like (e.g. Jensen the wrong way)
────────
[6/13] e.g. we tried to get it to improve the lower bound (which doesn't match the upper bound). I didn't have a construction in mind. It would suggest plausible, long arguments, but they all turned out to have errors. Wasted a good amount of time on that.
────────
[7/13] We also did experiments which we wouldn't normally do (and are unusual for a SODA paper) --- but they were super easy since we were already working in Windsurf. You can just describe the experiments in english and it already has the context of the setup from the paper.
────────
[8/13] Finally once we had a first draft we moved to overleaf, took a pass over the mathematical sections by hand (checking correctness again, but also organizing things in ways that made more sense), and finally wrote all the exposition (intro, etc) by hand.
────────
[9/13] It should go without saying that this is already the biggest change in the manner in which I do research in my career so far.
────────
[10/13] This was a successful enough experiment that I think it will be my standard workflow going forward --- though I'm cognizant that the tools are improving all the time and I'll need to be ready to adopt new ones as things change.
────────
[11/13] One more thought: AI tools are a very useful research accelerator for an expert, and I plan to use them whenever I can. But at the moment it is very easy to be led down false paths if you let them get ahead of yourself and lure you too far from your expertise.
────────
[12/13] Educating the next generation of researchers in the presence of these tools will be interesting. How do we teach students to be sufficiently expert that they can use the tools productively in the presence of these tools? How does one learn expertise? There will be answers but
────────
[13/13] It might require new pedagogical habits.

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (15 tweets)
summary:
[1/15] 2025 was an eventful/disruptive year for computer science research, for two reasons: 1) a shock to federal funding, and 2) the arrival of AI models capable enough to assist mathematical research. 1) is unambiguously bad and 2) is probably mostly good. I'll write about AI first.
────────
[2/15] Starting in the fall (Gemini 2.5 pro launched experimentally at the end of March) LLMs that were useful for math launched. I didn't have much luck using them within their web interface, but I found them to be extremely useful within coding agent harnesses like Windsurf.
────────
[3/15] This setup substantially accelerated writing math. I could "verbally" sketch an argument as if to a colleague, and the tools could turn that into a formally written lemma/theorem with proof. The proof was correct maybe 75% of the time, but could quickly iterate to correctness.
────────
[4/15] This summer I spent lots of time using these tools, and we wrote a couple of papers with them. The tools had a couple of memorable flashes of insight that simplified things, but for the most part it felt like accelerating writing the same paper we would have written without them.
────────
[5/15] In the late summer and spring, GPT 5 (and then 5.1 and 5.2) launched. The GPT 5/5.1/5.2 pro model seemed again like another step change. I again spent a lot of time with it. It could provide real complements to my expertise and work through long and complicated lines of reasoning
────────
[6/15] We wrote a paper that I think is substantially different/better than the one we would have written without it (coming soon)! This is still far from autonomous science --- working with these tools is like collaborating with a broadly educated, smart but error prone colleague.
────────
[7/15] The models still have many weaknesses. They are too optimistic about correctness. When they recall results from the literature, they misremember them as broader than they are (forgetting important pre-conditions). They do not have good sense for what theorems are interesting.
────────
[8/15] Nevertheless, the last 8 months have changed how I do research much more fundamentally than any other time during my career. This makes it very difficult to project forward. What will research at the end of 2026 look like? 2027? All I can confidently predict is "different".
────────
[9/15] We need to figure out how to educate the next generation of researchers. I feel I have strong research intuition that is complementary to the strengths of AI tools. But how did I get it? I think I developed it by struggling through calculations and failed proofs in grad school.
────────
[10/15] But AI tools are now very good at the "standard" calculations and proof techniques I struggled through. We will need to be more intentional about teaching these skills to young researchers, just as we teach arithmetic in school without the use of calculators.
────────
[11/15] (Current) AI tools are much less useful without the right intuition about what can and cannot work. When they are able to lure you away from your expertise, they can easily tempt you to believe that fatally flawed constructions can be made to work. Formal verification would help.
────────
[12/15] A world in which clever discoveries happen in data centers, and the role of the professional researcher is careful verification and due diligence is a world in which the job of researcher is much less fun. Many fewer people with choices would want this job, given the other costs.
────────
[13/15] I also worry about removing joy. The academic bargain is that extremely talented researchers forgo high industry pay and location freedom in exchange for a really -fun- job --- solving research puzzles for a living. The joy of the work is an important part of the bargain.
────────
[14/15] And we are already seeing that reducing the time and effort needed to produce "a paper" (not a -good- paper) is going to destabilize our existing institutions for peer review. We need to figure out how to manage researcher attention at scale and not be drowned in research slop.
────────
[15/15] So many things will change --- I'm convinced that AI will be transformative for mathematical research. I think the changes will go beyond the day-to-day, and will extend to how we train our students and how we disseminate our work. The future is exciting and uncertain.

[1/5] Neural networks are highly non-convex, so approximate error minimizers need not look anything like each other in parameter space. But we show that nevertheless (for many model sizes) approximate error minimizers must closely agree in function/prediction space despite this!

[1/4] How many samples do you need from an unknown distribution in order to train a model with multicalibration error at most epsilon?
Answer: 1/epsilon^3 samples is both necessary and sufficient.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGq6E6mWEAA0e80.jpg

[2/4] Paper here:
Joint work with the great @natalie_collina @LuJiuyao and Georgy Noarov.

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGq64LjW4AAw2p9.jpg

- Multicalibration requires substantially more samples than marginal calibration.
- Unlike marginal calibration, multicalibration is just as hard to obtain in the batch setting as the online setting.

- The upper bounds are randomized.

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] We have a new online boosting algorithm which is very efficient and effective. Unlike prior algorithms which maintain many weak learners and ensemble them, we operationalize the "dual view" of boosting. We don't maintain an ensemble. We try to construct an online hard core set.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPrluuQWAAA0W6q.png
────────
[2/7] The weak learning assumption is that there is no such distribution - so if it holds, by contrapositive, our error was low. Adding one more orthogonality condition also lets us compete with any predictor in the span of the weak class - the usual gradient boosting guarantee.
────────
[3/7] We make probabilistic forecasts that are multiaccurate wrt the weak class---i.e. with residuals orthogonal to the weak class. If we have high error, then ex-post reweighting by our own residual error gives a smooth distribution on which no weak learner has non-trivial edge.
────────
[4/7] In the end we're putting a bunch of existing pieces together. The fact that multiaccuracy implies weights for a hard core distribution was noticed by @SiCaPu, Dwork, and Vadhan. Lots of good prior work gave online adversarial algorithms for multiaccuracy and related notions.
────────
[5/7] Standard online learning tricks let us make this guarantee adaptive --- i.e. we get the boosting guarantee on every sub-interval on which the weak learning condition holds, even if it doesn't on others. This works through an adaptive version of a hard core distribution.
────────
[6/7] So we get two incomparable boosting guarantees in one. And the algorithm works well, matching or beating the best comparator on real and synthetic datasets. Since we don't maintain an ensemble we run ~ 50x faster than these competitor algorithms as well.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HProWniWwAAiKds.jpg

title: Aaron Roth (@Aaroth) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] Codex and Claude Code have a neat auto approve feature where 1) it doesn't ask for permissions, but 2) you get to feel safe. Well --- do you? The premise is it is asking an agent for permission. But if you don't trust the driver agent, why should you trust the review agent?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQWCH_WAAAnNZF.png
────────
[2/9] We study this and model both you (the principal) and the reviewer agent(s) as having utility functions you are trying to maximize. The driver agent repeatedly proposes actions. The reviewer agents compare them to a baseline and vote to approve or deny based on perceived utility.
────────
[3/9] What about long running agents? We study an MDP model where utilities depend on action and state and actions change state. We again get a characterization The performance difference identity lets us lift the one-shot conic-hull characterization (on Q values) to the full MDP.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQdHK5XkAIQDaP.jpg
────────
[4/9] There is a remarkably clean characterization of when you can. We start with a simple one-decision model. A system is safe if and only if the Principal's utility is in the non-negative span of the reviewer's utilities. The forward direction is elementary; backwards is LP duality.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQcmOrXIAAK6Av.jpg
────────
[5/9] The difficulty is reviewer agents are misaligned - their utility functions differ from yours. Can you still guarantee that the system is safe, even with an arbitrary driver agent? Safe means that principal utility is guaranteed to be no worse than following the baseline policy.
────────
[6/9] We call this condition "coalitional alignment" -- it is very similar to the market alignment condition that drives our earlier work: It is a substantially weaker condition than individual alignment (That the reviewer agents have your utility exactly)
────────
[7/9] What about strategic agents? Let both the driver agent and the reviewers be fully strategic and optimizing for their long run discounted payoff. Under the same non-negative span condition, every Nash equilibrium of the game is safe for the Principal--i.e. no worse than baseline.
────────
[8/9] Our paper is here: comments welcome! This is joint work with the wonderful @sikatasengupta @natalie_collina and @SurbhiGoel_
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQh5K5XUAARkfP.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQh8j0WQAA4Jgf.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQiDC9WMAAb7R1.jpg
────────
[9/9] But despite being weaker it is not guaranteed to be satisfied. Still, we find some preliminary evidence of non-trivial safety/completeness tradeoffs among real reward models, and these effects come from coallitional rather than individual alignment.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSQe2MPXgAA_o8o.jpg

Aaron Roth is speaking about how to get alignment from misaligned AI systems, which means making AI agents act in ways that match human goals even if their internal models are imperfect. He gave most of this talk recently at Cornell.

He will present again at RESI/MIT and the Harvard CS Colloquium. The talk covers how AI alignment research aims to ensure AI systems behave safely and usefully as they take on more important tasks in the world. A video of the talk is also available.

linked_urls.summary: Title: From (Mis)aligned Models to Aligned Systems Speaker: Aaron Roth, the Henry Salvatori Professor of Computer and Cognitive Science at the University of Pennsylvania Abstract: The world is being reshaped around AI as we watch. In the near future --- and already today --- many increasingly important tasks will be delegated to AI agents. The field of AI alignment studies how we can make AI models trustworthy --- faithful agents that advance the interests of their users. But alignment might be hard. In this talk we ask what we might be able to guarantee from systems --- either naturally emerging from markets, or intentionally desgined --- that consist of multiple AI models that are each individually mis-aligned. We will see that sometimes we can still guarantee good outcomes by leveraging a diversity of misalignment --- models that are misaligned with their user, but also with each other. This talk is based on a number of joint works with Natalie Collina, Surbhi Goel, Meena Jagadeesan, Michael Kearns, Sophia Pi, Emily Ryu, Sikata Sengupta, and Mirah Shi, powered by Concept3D Event Calendar Software
